boisterous

/BOY-stur-uss/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Boisterous means loud, energetic, and exuberant in a cheerful, high-spirited way that can spill into rowdiness.

The boisterous night market roared with vendors' calls, sizzling grills, and kids racing between the stalls.

Example

The trainer's 'calm greetings' lesson lasted about ninety seconds. Then the retriever puppies discovered the tug ropes, and the gym exploded into happy barking, skidding paws, and one overturned water bowl. "Every beginner class is this boisterous," the trainer shouted over the noise, laughing. "Loud, thrilled, and slightly out of control."

The joyful barking, skidding paws, and overturned bowl — noisy, exuberant near-chaos — capture exactly what boisterous means.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

rowdy: Rowdy means noisy and disorderly -- the noise has tipped into real misbehavior: shoving, breaking things, ignoring every call for order. Boisterous is loud and energetic too, but in a cheerful, good-natured way; a boisterous party is still fun to be at, while a rowdy one has guests you want to throw out.

rollicking: Rollicking means exuberantly lively and fun -- a rollicking comedy or party sweeps everyone along in carefree high spirits, and the word is pure compliment. Boisterous shares the energy but centers on volume and near-chaos, and it can carry a mild edge of 'a bit much.' Rollicking is fun described fondly; boisterous is loudness that may need settling down.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

subdued: quiet and restrained

calm: peaceful and untroubled

Where it sits · how loud and wild the energy gets

lively → boisterous → riotous

lively vs. boisterous: Lively means pleasantly energetic; boisterous adds real volume and a touch of rowdiness to that energy.

riotous vs. boisterous: Riotous goes beyond boisterous — noise and wildness so extreme they border on genuine chaos.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — boisterous: rough, unrefined (Middle English boistous; ultimate origin unknown)

Put it together: Boisterous comes from the Middle English word boistous, meaning 'rough or unrefined,' but the trail goes cold there — no one knows for certain where boistous itself came from. With no productive Latin or Greek root to branch from, there is no cognate quiz here; the word survives as its own noisy self, its rowdy meaning intact for six centuries.

Use the root in a new word: boisterously: The crowd cheered boisterously all night — the adverb is built directly on boisterous itself, since the word's deeper roots are lost to history.

Word Building

Word Choice

informal-to-neutral; fits groups, events, and people

Boisterous is about volume and rowdy exuberance and happily describes whole crowds, parties, or classrooms, while vivacious (also in this unit) is quieter praise for one person's charming social sparkle; boisterous can also carry a mild edge of 'a bit much.'
